name: Momogun, Rungus dialect
confidence_why: Forschner's 1994 grammar puts stress on the penultimate syllable of the stem, so that it shifts under prefixes, enclitics and article-substantivised verbs, but the same author's 2014 learner's booklet tells readers that no syllable receives stress, and nothing else read (King 1984, Banker & Banker 1984, Appell & Appell 1961, Lobel 2013) says anything about Rungus stress.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (Corel PDF 2009, 45 pp., title page "Hoturan di Boros Momogun (Rungus) / Outline of a Momogun Grammar (Rungus Dialect) by T.A. Forschner 1994 Kudat" = Glottolog ref 319207). Sec. 1.6O "The stress" is at printed pp. 11-12 = pp. 11-12, as stated. Every sentence of the quote is present verbatim in a fresh extracted text of pp. 11-12 (including the "stres s" typo); the compiler "[..]" elisions and "/" separators are the only textual differences. One substantive omission: the PDF marks the stressed syllable by UNDERLINING in the example words (visible only in the rendered page, dropped by extracted text), so the and the compiler quote carry no stress marks. Read from 300-dpi renders: 1.61 "…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the stem (root). With prefixation the author says it 'can retract' to the antepenultimate syllable of the word (examples anaru, opodok, mana'ud), though other prefixed forms keep penultimate stress (monulung, tumabang, avagat) and he admits 'quite a diversity' even within one stem. Enclitics such as -po can pull stress onto the final syllable (opodok-po). A prenasalized verb nominalized by the article it takes primary stress on its first syllable (it mananom 'the planter'). No minimal pairs or length correlate are given; stress is described as non-distinctive positional prominence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; 'primary stress' is mentioned once (1.63) implying a secondary degree exists, but no placement rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Retraction to antepenult in some prefixed forms; enclitic-induced final stress (opodok-po); first-syllable primary stress in article+prenasalized-verb nominalizations; 'quite a diversity when stressing, even in the same stem' (ara'at/kara'atan/mongindara'; tumabang/atabang/katabangan). The same author's 2014 pedagogical Teach Yourself Rungus (pp. 5, 7) tells learners 'One does not give any syllable a [special] stress or emphasis', which conflicts with the 1994 sketch and suggests stress is weak.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level, illustrated with citation forms of roots and their affixed derivatives; 1.64 'the tune of some sentences' gives sentence intonation separately.
new_statements.identity_note: Forschner describes the Rungus dialect of 'Momogun' (autonym) spoken on the Kudat and Bengkoka peninsulas, i.e. rung1259 proper; he separates the Gonsomon dialect (l > x) and, in 2014, says Gonsomon, Nulu and Tobilung differ 'only in a few alterations in pronouncing'. Ethnologue/Wikipedia lump Kimaragang (kima1244), Tobilung (tobi1239) and Rungus as one 'Momogun' language; Glottolog keeps rung1259 separate, and the statement applies to Rungus (Kudat) itself. King 1984 gives 86-96% shared cognates across 12 Rungus villages, so dialect variation is minimal.

readall_conflicts: Neither of the two listed works yielded a stress statement (one is a wrong item, one is silent), so the reading rests on the existing statement from Forschner 1994 (Hoturan di Boros Momogun, sec. 1.6O-1.63, pp. 11-12, held by the project): 'generally the stress lies with the penultimate of the stem', retracting to the antepenult of the prefixed word (i.e. staying on the stem penult) in many prefixed forms, with enclitics sometimes shifting stress to the ultima (opodok-po), article-substantivised prenasalised verbs stressed on the first syllable, and 'quite a diversity when stressing, even in the same stem'. The one disagreement in the file set is Forschner's own later pedagogical booklet Teach Yourself Rungus (2014, pp. 5 and 7, held by the project): 'One does not give any syllable a [special] stress or emphasis' — a learner's instruction that reads as 'no strong word stress', in tension with the 1994 grammar's penultimate rule from the same author. The 1994 grammar is the descriptive source and its examples mark stressed syllables, so it is taken as the statement of record; the 2014 remark is best read as a warning against English-style heavy stress rather than a phonological claim.

sources.citation: Forschner, T. A. 2014. Teach Yourself Rungus / Tudukai-no i kondiri do Rungus. Filderstadt (lessons written 2012; PDF 2014; 70 pp.).
sources.note: Pedagogical note repeated on pp. 5 and 7: 'there is no difference between spelling and pronouncing. The person has only to keep in mind: One does not give any syllable a [special] stress or emphasis.' Same author as the 1994 grammar; reads as a reading-aloud instruction (no strong stress), and sits uneasily with the 1994 sec. 1.60. The appended grammar outline lists '1.6O The stress' in its table of contents only.
